Board and Administrative Advisory Committee update. Tonight, we'll be hearing, from the School Board Advisory Committee, the Minority Student Achievement Advisory Committee.And we'll receive an update from Miss Erin Kunkel, our MSAC chair. Welcome back, Miss

Kunkel. Good evening, Chair Chandler, members of the school board, Superintendent Spence, and community members. My name is Erin Kunkel, and I am honored to serve as chair of the Minority Student Achievement

Advisory Committee. Tonight, I'm pleased to present MSAC's school year twenty twenty-five/twenty twenty-six update to the board. Our theme this year is Building Foundations Together. This phrase means that we are committed to working together, showing up for students and families, focusing on steady, essential work that lasts. Tonight, I'm happy to share how that commitment has taken shape in

practice. Next slide, please. At the heart of MSAC's work is our mission: to partner with Loudoun County Public Schools, parents, and the community to acknowledge and promote the needs of minority students by building a school system that is culturally and socially competent and positioned to provide fair and equitable learning experiences for all students. Next slide, please.

Equity is not about serving some students at the expense of others. It is about ensuring that every child in this division has what they need to succeed. This school year, MSAC made a deliberate decision to look inward before looking outward. We paused and reflected and asked ourselves, "Are we equipped? Are we prepared in the way that we need to be to do this work well?" That reflection led us to three

focus areas: recommitting to the core role of an MSAC delegate, strengthening our structure, training and engagement, and deepening student engagement and their sense of belonging. You cannot build strong foundations for others if your own foundation is unstable, so we started there. Next slide. With that foundation in mind, I would like to walk you through the concrete ways we have been building capacity and making an impact across the division this

year. Next slide. One of our most meaningful investments has truly been in our delegates. We introduced structured onboarding and men-mentorship so new delegates felt welcomed, guided, and supported rather than having to figure things out on their own. We sharpened how delegates engage in policy analysis, grounding that work in real student experiences. For example, we've asked the question, "What do policies mean

for a seventh grader who does not see themselves represented in the curriculum?" Or, "How does a family navigating a discipline process feel when they do not fully understand?" To support this, we partnered with the Division of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Accessibility and with Dr. Tyler to offer training focused on becoming better equity-oriented change agents. Our delegates are not just attending meetings, they are learning how to

advocate, how to move inside their institutions, and how to create change at the school level. We have also provided clear action pathways so that when delegates return to their schools, they know what to do and who to meet with. Meet with your principal. Meet with the equity leads at your school. Get on your PTO or PTSA agenda. Share MSAC updates and the meeting minutes. And we encourage them to engage with us on policy matters. Next

slide. Our delegates have shown up. What you see in these images from some of our meetings is not a committee going through the motions. It is a committee member and a community of s-delegates in the room at the tables doing the real work. This is what it looks like when our community shows up for its students, and we are proud of every delegate who has walked through those doors this year. Next slide.

MSAC's role also includes providing feedback on board policies, and this year we took that responsibility very seriously. Our delegates have reviewed and provided structured feedback on twenty-three board policies this year. Each one is examined through an equity lens and with the question: how does this policy affect minority students and all students and their families? We remain committed to centering equity in every policy conversation, keeping students and families in the forefront rather than as an

afterthought, and maintaining early and transparent communication with the school board and division leadership so we can continue to be trusted partners and collaborators and not just a checkbox in the process. Next slide. I would also like to speak directly to what our community has brought to us this year. The concerns we hear from families have clustered around four areas: racial slurs and hate speech,

disproportionate outcomes for minority students, students' sense of belonging or the lack of it, and access to ac-advanced academic programs and pathways. What I hope is clear is that when I s-name these four concern areas, that I am not talking about isolated complaints. We are seeing similar patterns across grade levels, schools, and backgrounds. Many families do not come to MSAC in a moment of calmThey come to us when something has gone wrong for their

student, when there has been a harmful incident, a discipline decision that they do not understand, or a missed opportunity they worry will close doors later. By the time they reach us, they are often tired of repeating their story and unsure if raising concerns will make a difference. What they say they want most is straightforward information, someone to validate what they are seeing is real, and a partner who can point

them towards the next step. That is the role we play in MSAC, not to replace school processes, but to help families navigate them and to ensure their experiences and the patterns that we hear about and we see inform the work at division level. In response, MSAC has created a space for families to share those experiences. We have connected them with resources and information, presentations to help them navigate systems that can feel

inaccessible or even overwhelming, and encouraged and equipped parents to advocate for their own children and for other families within their schools. We have continued to invest in our delegates and into the families that join us so that the people closest to the schools, the parents, families, and students, are prepared and have a great way to respond. There is more work to do, but families should know that MSAC sees them, we hear them, and we are not standing still, and we are not giving up on

this work. Next slide. One of our clearest priorities has been growing the representation and voice of MSAC. This year, thirty-six MSAC delegates have participated in general body meetings representing schools across the division. Last year, we had representation from roughly eighty percent of schools. That's significant progress, but it is not where we wanna be. I met last year with Dr. Spence and Assistant Superintendent

Dr. Ellis Williams, and from that meeting, Dr. Spence issued a clear call to action. Every school should have and needs to have at least one s- MSAC delegate. We are eager to continue that work and to reach that goal. We want to partner with division leadership to act on that and to strengthen recruitment pathways, improving mentorship, and increasing student delegate participation because students must have a voice in conversations about their own education.

Our goal is simple and it's ambitious. We would like one delegate, one MSAC delegate in every Loudoun County public school, and we are treating that as a shared goal between MSAC and division leadership. Next slide. Building foundations together isn't a slogan. It is a description of the patient, persistent, and collaborative work of change. Next

slide. As we look ahead, MSAC will continue to expand delegate representation, sustain equity-centered policy engagement, and support families through access, information, and advocacy. We are committed to strengthening our partnership across the division and continuing to collaborate in numerous and continued new ways because this work is always better when we do it together. On the horizon, we are excited to bring our community together next week on

Wednesday evening at Better Together, our family dinner and social. And then we are excited to join together again on Saturday, May ninth, to celebrate the students, teachers, administrators, staff, and MSAC delegates who make this equity work possible. We are also preparing for school year twenty twenty-six twenty twenty-seven executive board election, and we will continue with our delegate body meetings, and we are also going to beginning launching our member MSAC membership drive with the

ongoing goal of inviting more families and more secu- school communities and community members into this work alongside us. Next slide. I would like to close with this. MSAC exists because the community believes that every student, regardless of race, background, religious identity, or zip code, deserves to be seen, supported, and set up to succeed, and every student deserves to achieve

their dreams. We are truly grateful for the opportunity to serve in that mission and grateful to the school board and to the division for your partnership, collaboration, and willingness to listen. On behalf of the MSAC Executive Board, the MSAC delegates, and the families who trust us to carry their voices and their stories, I say thank you, and I am welcome to answer any questions you have. presentation. It's nice to have you back. Thank you. committee was stood up, the work that we did in the past, the work we currently do now, and just reminding them of the things. Like, we tell them straight out the gate, "You don't get to come in and demand that something gets changed right here, right now." But we ask them to be a collaborative partner, to be a support system. I always encourage the delegates, "Show up in your school and just ask how can you help." Sometimes it is... My previous experience was cutting open popsicles at a school event, and people cutting open popsicles made me a familiar face, which made me a resource and a connection for them to do

that, and so that's what we encourage delegates to do. Every school has a different culture and a different system, so we have to remind them that one size doesn't fit all. I wish I could hand you a book and a flyer and say, "This is how you do MSAC," but that wouldn't be beneficial to the diverse population and the diversity within our division. So we encourage them to approach it as who you are. What I do might not work for another, another delegate, might not work for our vice chair, but everyone has a way to connect, and we encourage

them to focus on that and lean into making meaningful connections. And how are they appointed? Um, the delegates are-- They fill out an application. Usually, the process goes that either the PTO leader or the PTSA leader, in, sends out a call and asks for delegates to sign up or anybody to volunteer to become a delegate. If the PTSO does it and the parent would, or the principal would like to volunteer a parent or nominate a parent, they can send an application,

and it's a digital application that we have, and all they have to do is request it. When they fill it out, the minute it's submitted, I get an alert, and I see that it's submitted. We review the application. If there's something missing like, what's your school or did you check in with your principal or your PTO, we try to encourage delegates to make sure that they at least talk to the PTO leadership or their principal, so they're not just volunteering out of the blue. We wanna make that connection. And then from there, we don't-- There's no interview process.

There's nothing like that. It's like, "Hey, you signed up, so we'll take you. Join us. You said you wanted to volunteer, so you're stuck with us now." And then from there, we lean in together, and we do the work. But we wanna keep it simple and streamlined. We don't wanna discourage people from joining us in the, in the work and joining us as delegates. It got to December, and we were just like , "What do we do?" And I had a meeting just to follow up with Dr. Ellis Williams, and we were like, "You know what would be great? Would you like to come to this event? You should join us. And so I feel like just reminding

people that you can come to a place and not feel judged, not feel picked at, and just be yourself and be who you really are is great, and I feel like it's an honor to be able to host something like that and bring that to division and know that it's different. Um, I believe that when MSAC was originally stood up, the idea was to deal with the, the racial disparity and the racism

that had been prevalent in LCPS up until a certain point. And with the attorney general's finding, it was determined that changes needed to be made in LCPS, and part of that was MSAC being stood up, not as a watchdog, but as a partner, a collaborative partner, to work with the division to help highlight this because oftentimes the stories of minoritized and marginalized people don't get heard, or they're lessened or saying, "Well, that's great that happened, but all of these other

things are more important." And so when MSAC was stood up, it really was about advocating for an equity committee, someone to bring these concerns, to have these equity-based conversations and discussions about what was going on in the division. Now, as to MSAC's participation and overlap with the equity committee, we had, when the equity committee was stood up, we had three representatives on the board. That was, that was sustained and through the equity committee, and that was just so we could participate and be involved in

those conversations. It wasn't to take over. It wasn't anything like that. It was to continue to be a part of conversations. Our representatives on the equity committee, more often than not, their feedback on policy or on issues was aligned with what MSAC did. Our equity council or equity committee members would report back to us what they heard. They would share their findings. If we had something to report out, we would sometimes ask our delegates who represented us to say, "Hey, can you share this event going on?" Or, "Can you share this, this policy we're working on or these things that have come to our

attention?" And that was our way of communicating with the equity committee. Now, do I think that MSAC and the equity council, the new equity council, should join together? No, I do not. Because although our work is aligned and although we do line up in many ways, I think MSAC provides something unique and special, and the equity council, as it is just brand new, has the potential to provide something unique. I do see that there is going to be a long partnership and collaboration, but we are

parents, and we are in and out of these schools daily. We are-- We have connections to the community. We can relay information. There are oftentimes that parents don't wanna come and say, "Hey, I gotta talk to a school board member," but they would rather express their concerns to a delegate, somebody who's in there with them in

the experience. I've had experiences where parents talk to me because I am a delegate and not just because I'm MSAC chair, because they know that I know what's going on in the school. I'm a part of the school community. And oftentimes, if you don't have somebody who's in the thick of it with you and understanding, it's difficult. And so I would say no, I believe strongly that there should always be an MSAC, like I believe there should always be an equity council. And giving up that resource and that connection to the

community does a great disservice not only to this school board but to this division and, frankly, to our parents and students. So I would encourage the board to strongly consider supporting both MSAC and the equity com- equity council as individual entities but also giving us the space and room to collaborate because we do great things, and we do even better

things when we're together, and I'm excited, even in this time as chair, to support the equity council as it's been stood up.
